 Live .  11,572 viewing 11572 viewing Live page Updated 3 minutes ago Anthropic shares expected to jump at start of trading as AI firm makes stock market debut
 Summary
 AI firm Anthropic is listed publicly for the first time, with the stock market in New York now open
 According to data from the Nasdaq, share prices are set to open at $105 , a steep jump from the $83 set last night - take a closer look at some of the numbers here 
 The company behind AI product Claude was valued at $1.5tn (£1.14tn) after raising a record $81bn ahead of its stock market debut
 The flotation is being seen as a crucial test for the AI sector, with Anthropic the first purely AI-focused firm to sell shares publicly
 The seven founders who set up Anthropic in 2021 will become multi-billionaires - we've looked at why private companies decide to sell shares publicly here 
 Live Reporting
 Edited by Caitlin Wilson, Kieran Kelly and Sakshi Venkatraman, with Samira Hussein and Nathalie Jimenez reporting from Times Square
 Protesters gather outside Nasdaq MarketSite published at 16:25 GMT 16:25 GMT 
 Samira Hussain and Nathalie Jimenez 
reporting from Times Square, New York 
 Nothing says New York quite like a protest.
 The reasons that brought this small and mighty band of activists were varied, from the environment to AI in healthcare.
 Four people have been arrested.

 Anthropic listing comes as Federal Reserve expresses concern about growth of AI debt published at 16:20 GMT 16:20 GMT 
 Rachel Clun 
Business reporter 
 AI financing was a key feature of the Federal Reserve Bank’s last meeting - more broadly, there have been growing concerns about the large amounts of debt being taken on in the AI space.
 According to minutes from the Fed’s October meeting, where it decided to hold rates steady , the central bank noted concerns about the rapid growth of AI-related debt which was being financed through "complex and opaque" structures. 
 "Almost all participants commented on risks associated with a scenario in which the returns on AI investment turned out to be disappointing to investors," the bank said. 
 A few of the meeting’s participants also noted that "AI-related exposures were becoming increasingly concentrated among a small number of firms".

 Is Anthropic's IPO compatible with its 'safety-focused' constitution? published at 16:11 GMT 16:11 GMT 
 Freya Scott-Turner 
Live reporter 
 Image source, Eleanor Drage Image caption, Dr Eleanor Drage says that safe development by major AI companies is possible, but it's not happening at the moment
 Founded in 2021 by seven ex-employees of OpenAI, Anthropic has cultivated something of a reputation as "the good guy" of AI. 
 "If powerful AI is coming regardless, Anthropic believes it’s better to have safety-focused labs at the frontier," says its constitution. 
 But recently, former employees have accused Anthropic of neglecting this mission - including a researcher who previously told the BBC that workers were "genuinely frightened" about the speed of its advancements.
 Dr Eleanor Drage, a senior AI ethics researcher at the University of Cambridge, says the idea that Anthropic needs to win an "AI arms race" and out-build competitors in the name of responsibility is "a kind of hype fest" and a "narrative" to justify a risky pace of development. 
 The problem is the "culture of development", Drage tells me. AI companies "don't want to [slow down], because they don't know how. They're so terrified they'll lose their competitive edge". 
 Because public shareholders enter the mix, IPOs bring in a larger group of people who want to see big financial returns. Is this compatible with safety?
 "We have to believe that there is a compromise," says Dr Eleanor Drage, who notes that engineers say that safe AI development is possible if we're "temperate and moderate" about the systems we build. "But that's just not what's happening," she adds.

 Anthropic determined to be the 'good guys' of AI published at 16:06 GMT 16:06 GMT 
 Imran Rahman-Jones 
Technology reporter 
 While it wouldn’t explicitly say it out loud, Anthropic has always appeared keen to position itself as the "good guys" of the AI world.
 The company is set up as a Public Benefit Corporation, which means it tries to balance shareholder interest with its responsible AI charter.
 It has an unusual corporate structure, with a “Long-Term Benefit Trust” overseeing the company’s board to make sure it is considering the public interest.
 Anthropic also has its own in-house philosopher, Amanda Askell, who has had a big say over Claude’s personality and the company’s constitution. 
 Defenders of the company would point to its spat with the US military over the use of its products in combat situations as an example of where responsibility was prioritised over profit.
 But critics question how the firm’s constant catastrophic language tallies with its continued development of ever-advanced models.

 We can now bring you some pictures showing Anthropic's co-founders celebrating as the company officially went public earlier today.
 As a reminder, shares are being offered initially at $83 but we won't know the official trading price for a little while - read more about that here.

 Not everyone buys the Anthropic hype published at 15:44 GMT 15:44 GMT 
 Michelle Fleury 
New York business correspondent 
 Media caption, Watch: 'The company's big, but not that big', says Fisher Investments founder
 Just avoid the hype - that’s the advice from billionaire investor Ken Fisher, founder of Fisher Investments. 
 He has warned investors to be wary of Anthropic’s stock market debut.
With shares priced at $83 each, he believes the company is overvalued.
 He likened the maker of the Claude chatbot to a “rocket-based car going from 10 miles an hour to 430 miles an hour, driven by a brilliant 17-year-old”. 
 “The company's big, but not that big, and exploding and growing,” he told BBC Business Today’s Opening Bell. 
 His concern? That Anthropic is a young company, led by young executives who may lack the experience needed to navigate the challenges of such rapid growth and deliver on ambitions of this scale.

 Anthropic shares expected to soar to $105 when trading opens published at 15:37 GMT 15:37 GMT Breaking 
 Rachel Clun 
Business reporter 
 Demand is building for Anthropic shares, as we've been reporting. 
 According to data from the Nasdaq, shares prices are set to open at $105, a steep jump from the $83 set last night.
 Trading has not yet begun, and this price can shift ahead of the start of trading.

 Anthropic share value expected to jump about 26% when trading begins published at 15:31 GMT 15:31 GMT 
 Rachel Clun 
Business reporter 
 Huge demand for Anthropic shares could drive the share price over $100 as it begins trading later today, jumping about 26% above its debut.
 The debut price for shares was $83, but demand for shares exceeded the number of shares available in the lead up to today's public listing.
 It means that once those shares are available for public trade in the next couple of hours, the price is very likely to climb.
 There are widespread reports that the share price could open trading at around $105, but that could change through the morning.
 Anthropic shares, under the ticker symbol ANT , are expected to start trading around midday EST (17:00 GMT).

 Key findings from Anthropic's 335-page document on plans to go public published at 15:23 GMT 15:23 GMT 
 Image source, EPA Image caption, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei (centre left) has become a key figure in the current AI era
 As part of the process to get onto the New York Stock Exchange, Anthropic published its prospectus.
 This is a legal document that gives potential investors information about a company before they decide to invest. 
 As the first major stand-alone lab to go public, the 335-page document was our first glimpse into how major AI companies are spending and earning, and how they're structured. 
 Some key findings included: 
 It's making a loss: The company recorded net losses reaching $104bn this year up to September
 But revenue is growing: Anthropic's revenues have ballooned to $33bn in the nine months to September this year, as the market for its tools - designed to speed up processes including coding and digesting information - has grown
 "Risks to humanity": Though it said Anthropic's technology could bring "extraordinary" benefits - including in healthcare - the company warned of "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity" if it wasn't "developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards"

 Guarding against risks of AI is our priority, Anthropic co-founder says published at 15:12 GMT 15:12 GMT 
 Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Daniela Amodei, company co-founder, speaking ahead of Anthropic's IPO
 "Anthropic is an unusual company, some would say weird. And in fact, many have," says Daniela Amodei, kicking off her speech at Nasdaq in New York.
 Daniela Amodei, who is a co-founder of Anthropic and sister to CEO Dario, spoke about the risks and concerns expressed about the future of AI.
 "AI can do incredible good in the world. It also carries real risks -- guarding against them has been our priority from day one," she says. 
 Since the company is a public benefit corporation, she says, they are "legally required to weigh the public good alongside returns to shareholders". 
 The co-founder then outlines a range of customers and use cases for Claude, from healthcare to education and production.
 We want Claude to be a "trusted partner," she says, but one who "leaves you in charge"
 Amodei then addresses "anyone watching who is uneasy about AI" and says that "this technology needs you, not your trust, but your voice".

 Amodei acknowledges AI concerns while celebrating debut published at 15:02 GMT 15:02 GMT 
 Image source, Getty Images Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei spoke briefly ahead of the stock exchange opening earlier today. 
 He spoke at length about the medical developments that are possible with Claude.
 "I believe sufficiently powerful AI working in construct with humans could compress a century of scientific and medical progress into a decade," Amodei said. 
 He also spoke about the concerns surrounding AI and safety, and said it had been a priority since the beginning, acknowledging, "the most difficult safety work lies ahead of us".
 The Anthropic co-founder said he would not bend to political or economic pressures. 
 "Today puts the company in a stronger financial position, and in doing so only strengthens our resolve to do the right thing," Amodei added.

 Shares are being offered at $83 - but that's just a starting point published at 14:49 GMT 14:49 GMT 
 As we've been reporting, the New York Stock Exchange has just opened for business.
 Shares are being offered at $83 each, but that's just a starting point.
 What we're waiting to see now is something called the trading price . This is the amount shares are being sold at in real time. 
 It may take several hours for this to be known. This is because an auction-like process must first take place, where all the orders to buy or sell stock are matched. A final price is then reached.

 Stock markets open up in anticipation of Anthropic trading published at 14:43 GMT 14:43 GMT 
 Rachel Clun 
Business reporter 
 US stock markets have opened in positive territory ahead of Anthropic’s first day of public trading. 
 The AI company already raised a record amount of money in its share sale , and will be one of the largest public companies on American stock exchanges. 
 The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index opened up nearly 2% at the start of trading and the S&P 500, which tracks the largest firms listed in the US, was up more than 1%.
 The Dow Jones Industrial Average was also up, about 0.3%.

 What is Anthropic's name on the stock market? published at 14:41 GMT 14:41 GMT 
 Image source, Bloomberg via Getty Images Image caption, ANT is the firm's abbreviated name on Nasdaq
 You may have noticed there are a couple of different names used to refer to Anthropic now it has gone public:
 ANT - this is the ticker symbol
 Anthropic PBC - this is the longer, more formal listing name
 Ticker symbols are abbreviated names used to identify all publicly traded shares of listed companies. 
 They are usually no longer than six characters - famous examples include TSLA for Tesla, F for the Ford Motor Company, and MSFT for Microsoft.

 What is an IPO and why do companies go public? published at 14:15 GMT 14:15 GMT 
 An initial public offering (IPO) is when a privately held company offers its shares to the public for the first time.
 In the case of Anthropic, which is set to debut on the US stock market today, members of the public will be able to buy and sell shares.
 These units of ownership in the company will give investors a stake in Anthropic's success, and comes with certain privileges such as voting rights in major financial or strategic decisions. 
 Why do businesses go public? 
 An IPO helps a company raise money to grow and allows early investors to sell their shares for a profit. 
 It can also allow a company access to more capital and help build brand awareness.
 Once a company is listed on an exchange, though, it is subject to greater regulatory scrutiny. It also has to meet certain reporting requirements, such as publishing public accounts.

 A closer look at some of the numbers behind Anthropic's public listing published at 14:10 GMT 14:10 GMT 
 Image source, Getty Images Anthropic has been valued at around $1.5 trillion (£1.14 trillion) ahead of its listing on New York's Nasdaq stock exchange.
 The company says it will offer the shares at $83 each, up from the proposed $70-$78 range, and will raise a record $81bn when it floats (goes public).
 Although the company's valuation is large, it is below the $2tn some backers of Anthropic predicted in the summer.
 It is also below that of SpaceX - Elon Musk's rocket, satellite and artificial intelligence company - which listed its shares in June and was valued at nearly $1.8tn .
 Anthropic, which will list under the symbol ANT, will be the first fully AI-focused company to go public.

 How does a stock market debut work? published at 14:00 GMT 14:00 GMT 
 Rachel Clun 
Business reporter 
 Why are we able to say Anthropic has raised $81bn in its
stock market debut, when it hasn’t actually hit the stock market yet? And how
do we know its rough valuation already?
 When a company prepares to list on a stock
exchange, it goes through a lengthy process of providing details of its
finances, before drumming up interest from banks and investors in buying its
shares. 
 It usually sets an estimated share price, before going into
negotiations with those investors over purchases of those shares.
 When those deals are finalised, before the company goes
public, we get the final share price before trading begins - in this case,
$83.
 Those shares can’t be traded with other banks or investors
until trading begins, which is when Anthropic will officially become a public listed company. 
 That won’t happen as soon as the market opens at 09:30 EST (14:30 GMT) either - it
usually takes a little time for things to start working here.
